newsitem.title: JAPAN: Thai firm says Sumitomo to cut Thai copper sales.
newsitem.headline: Thai firm says Sumitomo to cut Thai copper sales.

text.p: Sumitomo Corp will stop supplying refined copper next year to one of Thailand's largest copper users, a top official at the Thai firm said on Monday.

Traders in Japan also noted talk that the trade house was pulling out of Thailand's refined copper trade entirely and cutting back in other markets as well, in the wake of its massive copper trading losses.

"Sumitomo doesn't look to supply any copper cathode in Thailand next year," said Sompong Nakorsri, president and chief executive officer of Bangkok Cable Co. He said his company produces 20,000 tonnes of copper cable per year.
A Sumitomo spokesman said the trade house would not comment on matters related to its transactions.
In a telephone interview, Sompong said Sumitomo had supplied more than 40 percent of Thailand's copper cathode.
Local industry sources expected Thailand's demand for refined copper to reach nearly 200,000 tonnes this year.
Sompong said Sumitomo had a bonded warehouse in Thailand from which it supplied its customers, although he said Sumitomo's prices were little different from those of other traders.
A Japanese copper trader at a leading Sumitomo rival said there was talk in the market that Sumitomo would stop maintaining its own copper stocks in Thailand.

Several Japanese copper traders also said that before Sumitomo's former chief copper trader Yasuo Hamanaka was fired in June for alleged illicit trades, the trade house sold copper at sizable discounts to customers both domestically and abroad. They speculated he covered losses from the discounts with gains from futures trading on the London Metal Exchange.

A purchasing source at a major Japanese copper user, however, countered that Sumitomo was offering copper at only marginally lower prices than its competitors were, adding that Hamanaka's advantages derived largely from the quicker, more reliable delivery made possible by selling from his own stocks.
Sumitomo accused Hamanaka of racking up $2.6 billion in losses from unauthorised trades. He has since been arrested on charges of fraud and forgery.

Although Thailand currently relies on imports for its refined copper, a 185,000-tonne-per-year refinery is due to begin operation in October 1998, with full production expected within a year after that.
